balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

customersUS.title: T-Mobile US customers
customersUS.content:
CustomersUS is T-Mobile US's total reported customer count (postpaid, prepaid and wholesale) in millions.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: T-Mobile US is the group's majority-owned growth engine and the main reason consolidated revenue and EBITDA have outgrown the mature German/European fixed base -- customers grew from 79.7m (FY2018) to 119.7m (FY2023) through aggressive postpaid net adds and the Sprint merger.

What to watch:

  • Postpaid net adds versus AT&T/Verizon (market-share trend)
  • Churn and ARPU alongside raw customer count -- growth funded by discounting is lower quality

germanFixed.title: Germany fixed-network mix
germanFixed.content:
Fixed lines are traditional copper/voice connections; broadband is fixed internet access (DSL/fibre/cable); mobile customers (Germany) is the domestic cellular base. All three are the German fixed-network segment, distinct from the blended global Subscribers/FixedLines columns elsewhere on this page.

For Deutsche Telekom AG: legacy fixed lines have been in structural decline (18.6m FY2018 to 17.3m FY2023) as customers migrate to broadband and mobile, but broadband has held broadly flat-to-growing (~21-22.5m) and German mobile customers have grown steadily (48.2m FY2020 to 74.5m FY2025) -- convergence (fixed + mobile bundles, fibre upgrades) offsetting the voice-line runoff rather than a shrinking domestic business.

What to watch:

  • Fibre/broadband net adds versus the fixed-line decline rate
  • Mobile customer growth sustaining ARPU, not just subsidised SIM-only adds
